title: Bayesian nested-error unit-level model
text:
The Fay–Herriot workbook starts from direct estimates. A unit-level nested-error model starts one step earlier, with the respondent records themselves. The model relates each respondent’s walking outcome to unit-level predictors and area effects, then aggregates the fitted model to MSOA–year means using known population auxiliary information.
In this workbook we keep the structure deliberately constrained. The response is still the daily walking indicator:
The three models are:
This is the same logic as the Battese–Harter–Fuller unit-level setup: fit the relationship using sampled units, then use known area means of the auxiliary variables to predict area means.

title: Bayesian nested-error unit-level model
text:
1 Prepare Modelling Data
The sample modelling file needs one row per respondent. For this constrained example we use:

freq_walker as the binary response;
wave_year for the temporal effect;
msoa_code as the nested area identifier;
car_access_code as the unit-level auxiliary predictor.

The National Survey for Wales variable CarUse is coded as whether a car or van is available for use. In the cleaned survey microdata it is retained as car_access_code, where 1 means yes and 2 means no. We convert it to a binary no_car predictor.

survey_microdata <- read_csv(
  file.path(base_path, "clean", "survey_microdata_msoa_year.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

unit_sample <- survey_microdata |>
  transmute(
    unit_id,
    domain_id = msoa_code,
    msoa_name,
    la_code,
    la_name,
    wave_year,
    freq_walker,
    no_car = case_when(
      car_access_code == "2" ~ 1,
      car_access_code == "1" ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    ),
    analysis_weight = freq_walker_weight
  ) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(.data$freq_walker),
    !is.na(.data$domain_id),
    !is.na(.data$wave_year),
    !is.na(.data$no_car)
  )

title: Bayesian nested-error unit-level model
Bayesian nested-error unit-level model
text:
3 Fit Models
The model is fitted as a linear probability nested-error model. This keeps the aggregation step transparent: for M2, the area-level predictor value is the known MSOA mean of the binary no_car variable. A logistic unit-level model would require aggregating predicted probabilities across the full population distribution of the unit-level predictors, which is useful but less aligned with the simple Battese–Harter–Fuller example.

m0_formula <- freq_walker ~
  1 +
  f(year_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid")

m1_formula <- freq_walker ~
  1 +
  f(year_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_spatial_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

m2_formula <- freq_walker ~
  no_car +
  f(year_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_spatial_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

model_formulas <- list(
  "M0 +Temporal" = m0_formula,
  "M1 +Spatial" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +No-car predictor" = m2_formula
)

fit_unit_model <- function(formula) {
  fit_data <- bind_rows(
    unit_model_data |>
      mutate(row_type = "sample"),
    unit_aggregation_data |>
      select(
        unit_id = domain_id,
        domain_id,
        msoa_name,
        la_code,
        la_name,
        wave_year,
        freq_walker,
        no_car,
        area_id,
        year_id,
        area_iid_id,
        area_spatial_id
      ) |>
      mutate(row_type = "prediction")
  )

  fit <- INLA::inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "gaussian",
    data = fit_data,
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, dic = TRUE)
  )

  prediction_rows <- which(fit_data$row_type == "prediction")

  predictions <- as_tibble(
    fit$summary.fitted.values[prediction_rows, , drop = FALSE]
  ) |>
    transmute(
      unit_estimate = mean,
      unit_lower = .data[["0.025quant"]],
      unit_upper = .data[["0.975quant"]]
    ) |>
    bind_cols(
      unit_aggregation_data |>
        select(
          domain_id,
          msoa_name,
          la_code,
          la_name,
          wave_year,
          raw_share_no_car_households
        )
    ) |>
    mutate(
      unit_estimate = pmin(pmax(.data$unit_estimate, 0), 1),
      unit_lower = pmin(pmax(.data$unit_lower, 0), 1),
      unit_upper = pmin(pmax(.data$unit_upper, 0), 1)
    )

  list(fit = fit, predictions = predictions)
}

unit_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_unit_model)

title: Bayesian nested-error unit-level model
text:
6 What Changes Across Models?
We compare the MSOA–year predictions across the three constrained models. M0 provides the temporal nested-error baseline, M1 adds spatial borrowing across neighbouring MSOAs, and M2 adds the no-car auxiliary relationship before aggregating at the MSOA no-car mean.


Code
unit_step_summary <- unit_estimates |>
  transmute(
    domain_id,
    wave_year,
    `M0 to M1` =
      .data[["unit_estimate__M1 +Spatial"]] -
      .data[["unit_estimate__M0 +Temporal"]],
    `M1 to M2` =
      .data[["unit_estimate__M2 +No-car predictor"]] -
      .data[["unit_estimate__M1 +Spatial"]]
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(`M0 to M1`, `M1 to M2`),
    names_to = "comparison",
    values_to = "estimate_change"
  ) |>
  group_by(.data$comparison) |>
  summarise(
    `Median absolute change` = pp_label(median(abs(.data$estimate_change), na.rm = TRUE)),
    `95th percentile absolute change` = pp_label(
      quantile(abs(.data$estimate_change), 0.95, na.rm = TRUE)
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

7 Final Unit-Level Estimate
The final constrained model is M2. It keeps the unit-level structure simple while demonstrating the central nested-error idea: fit a respondent-level auxiliary relationship, then use the known MSOA mean of that auxiliary variable to estimate the MSOA mean outcome.

        unit_estimate = `unit_estimate__M2 +No-car predictor`,
        raw_share_no_car_households

    by = "domain_id"

The model-based estimates are expected to be smoother than direct estimates because they borrow strength across respondents, years, and neighbouring MSOAs. The direct estimates remain useful as a diagnostic, but the unit-level model targets the area mean through the fitted respondent-level relationship and the known area mean of no-car access.

title: Bayesian nested-error unit-level model
text:
8 Unit-Level Versus Area-Level Models
The useful final comparison is not that one model is always better than the other. The point is that the two approaches use different information and therefore have different failure modes.
The Fay–Herriot model uses area-level direct estimates as the response. This keeps the survey-design work in the direct-estimation stage: the direct estimates and their sampling variances already reflect the weighted survey estimator. The unit-level nested-error model uses respondent records directly. That lets us model the individual response, but this basic version does not fully carry the complex survey design into the likelihood. As a result, it can be more sensitive to sample composition, sparse within-area samples, and any mismatch between sampled respondents and the auxiliary population means.

fh_final_estimates <- read_csv(
  file.path(base_path, "freq_walker_estimates_fh_inla.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  filter(.data$model == "M4 +Spatial") |>
  transmute(
    domain_id,
    wave_year,
    fh_estimate = fh_estimate,
    fh_variance = fh_variance

The comparison exposes the tradeoff. The area-level model is more tightly connected to design-based direct estimates and their sampling uncertainty. The unit-level model can use respondent-level relationships directly, but in this simple version it only uses no-car access and does not include age or sex. If age and sex are important predictors of walking, omitting them leaves residual composition differences inside the area effects.
Adding age and sex to the unit-level model changes the aggregation problem. We would no longer need only one MSOA mean for no_car; we would need a population table that represents the joint distribution of the predictors used for prediction, such as MSOA–year by age group and sex. That is the bridge to multilevel regression and poststratification: fit the richer unit-level model, then average predictions over the population cells. The next workbook takes that step.

We use survey::svyby() to compute the weighted share and its uncertainty diagnostics for every MSOA-year cell with usable observations. It then completes the MSOA-by-wave grid so missing cells are retained for modelling.

# Define survey design
walk_design <- survey::svydesign(
  ids = stats::as.formula("~1"),
  strata = stats::as.formula("~strata"),
  weights = stats::as.formula("~weight"),
  data = survey_walk
)

# Calculate direct estimate and uncertainty
direct_walk_estimates <- survey::svyby(
  formula = stats::as.formula("~indicator"),
  by = stats::as.formula("~domain_id + wave_year"),
  design = walk_design,

title: Direct Estimation
text:
2 Evaluate direct estimates
Direct estimation provides a useful starting point because they make three limitations visible:

Uneven temporal and spatial coverage: The number of usable observations varies across survey waves and across MSOAs. This means some MSOA-year estimates are based on much less direct evidence than others.
Unstable area estimate over time: For some MSOAs, direct estimates change sharply between waves. These changes may reflect real behavioural change, but they may also reflect sampling noise.
Zero within-area variance: For binary indicators, especially with small samples, some MSOAs show no within-area variation because all respondents give the same response. This can produce zero or unrealistically low variances.

title: Modelling Data Preparation
section: 1 Synthetic National Survey for Wales response datasets - 3 waves
text:
1 Synthetic National Survey for Wales response datasets - 3 waves
The tutorial uses a synthetic teaching dataset based on the National Survey for Wales (NSW). The NSW is a repeated cross-sectional survey of people in Wales, with annual survey periods covering topics such as transport, health, education, public services, housing, internet access, climate change, and the Welsh language. For this tutorial, the cleaned microdata combine three survey periods: 2020-2021, 2022-2023, and 2024-2025 into one harmonised survey microdata.
Since the survey responses are geo-indexed at the Local Authority level, but the practical tutorial estimates indicators at MSOA level, we use a synthetic MSOA assignment. The cleaned survey file keeps each respondent’s Local Authority and assigns a synthetic MSOA within that Local Authority using deterministic random allocation. As such, estimates produced from these data should not be read as substantive findings about individual MSOAs in Wales.
This design has two purposes:

Higher spatial resolution for tutorial purposes. The tutorial can demonstrate MSOA-level direct estimation, area-level SAE, spatial modelling, and MRP-style poststratification.
Privacy and disclosure protection. The assigned MSOA is not the respondent’s true MSOA, so the tutorial avoids presenting fine-grained respondent locations.




Synthetic areal disaggregation





Preparation pipeline for analysis-ready inputs

title: Modelling Data Preparation
text:
2 Defining the Estimand
It is important to define the estimand before proceeding to the next step. The estimand determines how we can formulate the appropraite indicator from survey variables, how we aggregate it to the desired area level, and which model inputs such as predictors and spatio-temporal structure are valid downstream. A well-formed estimand answers:

Estimate the measure of what outcome, among which population, across which geography and time period.

For the main tutorial, we use seek to perform SAE on estimand:

Outcome
Walks for transport daily

Adults

The target population definition is particularly important when we are estimating means or proportions since it determines the denominator for such aggregation. Moreover, it dictates the requirement for target population sizes or poststratification tables when formulating the models.

title: Modelling Data Preparation
text:
4 Preparing auxiliary data

4.1 Area Predictors
Area-level SAE needs covariates that plausibly explain spatial differences in daily walking. The area predictors drawn from Census 2021 bulk tables at MSOA level. The table keeps raw variables for interpretation and z-scored cov_* variables for modelling.
These variables are chosen because daily walking is likely to vary with density, car access, commuting mode, housing form, and the socioeconomic and student composition of each area.







Variables
Why include




Population density
Denser urban areas tend to be more walkable


Share of households without car/van
Individual no-car households tend to walk, cycle, take public transport more


Working from home, Full-time students and routine/semi-routine occupations
Individual occupation may explain their propensity to walk





4.2 Poststratification Table
A population poststratification table is needed to apply the fitted unit-level model to the target population. Because the estimand is the share of adults who walk for transport daily, the tutorial uses an MSOA-by-year-by-age-by-sex population table.
We built our poststratification tables from ONS MSOA quinary age-by-sex population estimates and keeps the survey years used in this tutorial: 2021, 2023, and 2025. A few notes on the preparation of the poststratification tables:

The youngest available ONS age band is 15 to 19. This is used as the closest available population cell for the 16+ walking estimand.
For MRP, the variables that define poststratification cells must be available in both the survey and the population table, with compatible categories.

Note that other useful predictors can still enter the unit-level model as area-level predictors. For example, population density and no-car households are joined by MSOA. They help explain spatial differences in walking, but they do not need to define additional poststratification cells.

Before fitting the models, we create a consistent numeric index for each MSOA and survey year. These indices are used by INLA to attach random effects to the correct area and period.

area_levels <- sort(unique(model_data_raw[["domain_id"]]))

  domain_id = area_levels,
  area_id = seq_along(area_levels)
)

year_index <- tibble::tibble(
  wave_year = year_levels,
  year_id = seq_along(year_levels)
)

To include a spatial random effect, we also need an adjacency graph .adj as input. We use Queen contiguity, where two MSOAs are treated as neighbours if their boundaries touch at either an edge or a point. The boundary file is sorted using area_index so that the graph order matches the area IDs used in the modelling data.


msoa_boundaries_sorted <- msoa_boundaries |>
  dplyr::inner_join(area_index, by = "domain_id") |>
  dplyr::arrange(.data$area_id)

  msoa_boundaries_sorted,
  queen = TRUE,
  row.names = msoa_boundaries_sorted$domain_id
)

spatial_graph_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".adj")

spdep::nb2INLA(
  file = spatial_graph_file,
  nb = msoa_neighbours
)

We then assemble the modelling data. The models use two area-level random-effect structures, so we create separate INLA index variables:

area_iid_id indexes the unstructured, independent area effect.
area_spatial_id indexes the structured spatial area effect, which uses the adjacency graph.

Lastly, the sampling variance also needs careful handling before fitting the FH models with INLA. The extent to which the noisy direct estimates will be stablised depends on their sampling variances.

For MSOA-year small areas without a direct estimate or variance, we assign the maximum observed positive sampling variance, signalling high uncertainty. Their estimates will be mostly model predictions.
Because the outcome is binary (1 for walking daily, 0 otherwise), very small samples can produce a variance of 0 when all sampled respondents give the same response. We also assign these cells the maximum observed positive sampling variance.


max_variance <- max(
  model_data_raw$variance[model_data_raw$variance > 0],
  na.rm = TRUE

      .data$variance <= 1e-8 ~ max_variance,
      TRUE ~ .data$variance

title: Bayesian Fay-Herriot area-level model
text:
2 Fit Models
Each model uses the direct estimate as the response. The sampling variance from the direct-estimation workbook is passed to INLA as known observation-level uncertainty, so cells with noisy direct estimates receive less weight.
We will fit five cumulative models:








Model
Name
Specifications




M0
Baseline
Intercept plus independent area effect


M1
+Temporal
M0 plus temporal random walk


M2
+Core predictors
M1 plus population density and no-car households


M3
+All predictors
M2 plus economic activities (full-time students, semi-routine/routine occupation, WFH)


M4
+Spatial
M3 plus spatial structure among MSOA adjacency



We define the model specifications and fit each one to the direct estimates using INLA.

m0_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  1 +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid")

m1_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  1 +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid") +
  f(year_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

m2_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  cov_population_density +
  cov_share_no_car_households +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid") +
  f(year_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

m3_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  cov_population_density +
  cov_share_no_car_households +
  cov_share_work_from_home +
  cov_share_students +
  cov_share_routine_semiroutine +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid") +
  f(year_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

m4_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  cov_population_density +
  cov_share_no_car_households +
  cov_share_work_from_home +
  cov_share_students +
  cov_share_routine_semiroutine +
  f(
    area_spatial_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  ) +
  f(year_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

model_formulas <- list(
  "M0 Baseline" = m0_formula,
  "M1 +Temporal" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +Core predictors" = m2_formula,
  "M3 +All predictors" = m3_formula,
  "M4 +Spatial" = m4_formula
)

fit_fh_model <- function(formula) {
  INLA::inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "gaussian",
    data = model_data,
    scale = 1 / model_data$sampling_variance,
    control.family = list(
      hyper = list(
        prec = list(initial = 0, fixed = TRUE)
      )
    ),
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
    control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE),
    verbose = FALSE
  )
}

model_order <- names(model_formulas)
fh_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_fh_model)

At this point the result is just a named list of fitted INLA models. We will collate the fitted values into one results table together with their original direct estimates and sampling variances.


Code
# Main frame to keep from model data
output_cols <- c(
  "domain_id",
  "wave_year",
  "msoa_name",
  "direct_estimate",
  "variance",
  "n"
)

model_output_frame <- select(model_data, all_of(output_cols))

# Extract fitted values from each model and bind them to the frame
fh_result_tables <- purrr::map2(
  fh_fits,
  names(fh_fits),
  function(fit, model_name) {
    fitted_values <- tibble::as_tibble(fit$summary.fitted.values)

    model_results <- bind_cols(model_output_frame, fitted_values)

3 Choose Model
Before we compare the models and modelled estimates, it is worth undesrtanding how the FH models fundamentally handle noisy direct estimates.
We start by comparing the direct estimates with M0, the baseline Fay-Herriot model with no area predictors, spatial structure, or temporal structure. MSOA-years with high sampling variance contain less reliable local information, so M0 pulls them more strongly toward its baseline prediction.

3.1 Model Comparison
Next, we use WAIC as a first check for comparing the model specifications. WAIC, returned by INLA, is a global predictive-fit measure: lower values indicate better expected prediction after penalising model complexity. This helps identify model specifications that are clearly weaker before we examine the remaining models in more detail.

  fh_fits,
  \(fit, model_name) {
    tibble::tibble(
      model = model_name,
      waic = fit$waic$waic,
      eff_params = fit$waic$p.eff
    )
  }
)

M0 is understandably weaker than the structured models because it has no predictors (-636.6415). M2 has the lowest WAIC (-642.5301), suggesting that the temporal term and the two core predictors, population density and car access, already capture much of the area-level variability. However, the differences among M1-M3 are small, so we treat them as having broadly similar predictive performance.
WAIC is useful, but it does not show where estimates change locally or whether those changes are substantive. For Fay-Herriot models, this matters because the aim is not only good overall prediction, but also stabilising noisy local estimates. When predictors are added, the model updates the expected value for each MSOA-year. Unstable direct estimates are then pulled more strongly toward those updated model predictions, which can improve local accuracy when the predictors are relevant.
For example, moving from M2 to M3 adds the occupation and work-pattern predictors. We map where M3 changes the estimates relative to M2, then summarise the predictor profiles of the areas with the largest upward and downward shifts (top and bottom 10%).

3.2 Assessing Temporal and spatial effects
The contribution of the temporal and spatial effects on the model prediction can be exmined through two diagnostic outputs by INLA:

tau is the precision of the random effect, or the inverse of its variance. A higher tau means the random effect varies less.
phi is the BYM2 mixing parameter: it indicates how much of the area random effect is assigned to the structured spatial component versus the unstructured component. A value of 0.5 means the structured and unstructured components contribute roughly equally to the area random effect.

The temporal effect has a high tau (6091.734), which means the model estimates only small differences between the three survey waves. The effect is still useful to include because it lets the model account for wave-to-wave changes insteading of treating survey responses from all waves as one.

3.3 Reporting final estimates and uncertainty
Choosing the final model therefore requires balanced judgement, combining performance diagnostics such as INLA’s WAIC with domain knowledge about the estimand. Where possible, model choice can also be strengthened through further benchmarking, such as comparison with related external indicators or sensitivity checks.
The final model estimates should be reported with their associated uncertainty. For transparency in downstream use of the output datasets, they should also be accompanied by relevant metadata, including the direct estimates, sample sizes, sampling variances, and the modelling specification used to produce them.

  filter(.data$model == "M4 +Spatial")

  left_join(final_model_results, by = "domain_id")
final_estimate_limits <- range(final_model_results$fh_estimate, na.rm = TRUE)
final_variance_limits <- c(0, max(final_model_results$fh_variance, na.rm = TRUE))
final_wave_years <- sort(unique(final_model_results$wave_year))

  final_map_data |>
    filter(.data$wave_year == wave) |>
    ggplot() +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data$fh_estimate), colour = "transparent") +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(
      option = "magma",
      limits = final_estimate_limits,
      labels = share_label,
      na.value = "grey85",
      name = "Share"
    ) +
    ggtitle(wave) +
    theme_void() +
    map_text_theme
}

    ) +

    theme_void() +
    map_text_theme
}

uncertainty_maps <- lapply(final_wave_years, plot_final_variance)

uncertainty_maps[[1]] <- uncertainty_maps[[1]] + ylab("Posterior variance")

The final maps illustrate why this matters: Even after the direct estimates have been stabilised through the Fay-Herriot model, weaker survey coverage can still leave unusual year-specific patterns in the modelled estimates. 2023 estimates are generally higher than in 2021 and 2025, likely due to that wave’s smaller sample size. For transparency, the 2023 estimates should therefore be read alongside their posterior uncertainty and the original sample sizes.
